title: A Well-Meaning Little Busybody
author: Mrs. L. G. Morse
first_words: They say I am full of mischief, but they don't speak the truth.
last_words: I am going to hurry fast, and see if I can get it done before mamma comes home from market.
cuts: Omit one whole paragraph, lines 1245-1250: from "Afraid! They're afraid of everything." to "tell me not to move 'till she'd cleared up the floor." (brings the piece under 650 words; it is the only cut)
why_good: The whole story is a small child's first-person account in which she believes she is the household's most useful helper, while every 'favor' she describes (the dropped basin, rags stuffed in papa's collar drawer, dust swept under mamma's dresses, about to cut the lace off mamma's best sleeves) is a disaster. The reader has to see past an unreliable narrator: the adults' remarks ('Maria says I'm a busybody', 'nobody else but just me would ever have thought of putting it away') are dry irony she takes as praise. Comic and deadpan in tone.
suitability: Read the whole piece (lines 1213-1270, it is complete and self-contained). Domestic comedy only; no caricature, dialect mocking a group, or cruelty. The omitted paragraph has the narrator cutting her hand on the broken basin (mild); removing it also removes the one injury.
fame: Mrs. L. G. Morse was an occasional Harper's Young People contributor; this is a one-page filler piece never anthologized as far as I know, under a byline nobody would recognize.

title: How Conrad Lost His School-Books
author: Walter Bobbett
first_words: After brushing the dust from his hair and his clothes, he followed
last_words: "Oh, the poor princess!" said he. "If only I had my key!"
why_good: Dramatic irony: a boy who has been reading fairy tales is sure the kitchen girl who pulls him out of a flour barrel is an enchanted princess, and that a lantern is a dragon's fiery eye. She offers him mince pie, has no idea what 'enchanted' means, and only wants him gone before she is punished. The reader has to keep two versions of the scene going at once (Conrad's and the real one), and the narrator's mock-solemn voice carries the comedy.
suitability: Read the whole story (lines 2492-2803). Slapstick only (an official pinches his ear, a duke drops him out of a low window, he falls into flour); it turns out to be a feverish dream. No caricature or cruelty. The excerpt explains itself: the key, the barrel and his belief in enchantment are all stated inside it.
fame: Walter Bobbett was a St. Nicholas illustrator who wrote and drew this one piece ('Illustrated by the Author' in the volume contents). Not a known author; the story has not been reprinted as far as I know.

title: Johnny's Lost Ball
author: Lloyd Wyman
last_words: For once in his life, Johnny felt as if the world had slipped from under him.
why_good: A small comedy of temptation told by a dry, amused narrator: a boy who goes out for a science book is talked into a second-hand copy by a bookseller with an opinionated folksy patter ('Steele biles his'n down'), and then is talked out of his change by the same man's rapid sales pitch for a ball ('children cry for 'em'). There are understated jokes to catch: 'dead broke financially, but happy, nevertheless', and the family 'were inclined to find fault with him, though I do not know why'. The excerpt ends on the ball dropping into the cistern pipe.
suitability: Read the whole story (lines 3946-4143). The rest is the schoolmaster showing him how to float the ball out with water. The bookseller's rural speech is one tradesman's idiom, not dialect used to mock a group. Nothing unsuitable.
fame: Lloyd Wyman appears only as a St. Nicholas byline; no known body of work. The piece is obscure.

title: Mother's Idea
author: A. M. Platt (the issue file prints no byline; the name is from the volume contents in pg32622.txt line 288: 'MOTHER'S IDEA. _A. M. Platt_ 613')
first_words: Mr. Atherton has been the master of the Centreville Academy ever since I
last_words: "I know, dear," Mother said, with a sigh; "but Father thinks he does what is best."
why_good: A first-person narrative by a girl of about fifteen whose father, worried about money, flatly refuses her seventy-five cents toward a class present. The reader has to read between the lines: her mixed envy and fairness toward the rich classmate, her hurt at her father's bluntness, the hint of the family's money troubles, and her sudden insight about her mother ('I wonder if she ever wishes for things she doesn't get'). The mother's sigh at the end is open to interpretation. The tone is earnest and wistful, quite unlike the P1 comedy. A shorter clean ending is line 3302 ('...never to do as the others do.'), which gives 547 words.
suitability: Read the whole piece (lines 3253-3464): the mother organizes a cheap party, the father designs a framed testimonial, and the narrator gains standing at school. Nothing unsuitable; no caricature.
fame: A. M. Platt is unknown outside this one St. Nicholas contents entry, and the piece is printed unsigned in the issue. Different magazine from the P1 primary (St. Nicholas, not Harper's Young People) and a different year (1886, not 1880).

title: XIII.--A Story of Two Buckets
author: Charlotte M. Vaile
first_words: There they were hanging, one of them out of sight in the cool, deep
last_words: when he sank under his grief and shame never to see any more bright days.
cuts: Cut 1, lines 3595-3605: from "\"I don't like this kind of a well at all,\" said Daisy." to "though she could not have told when."
Cut 2, lines 3634-3639: from "\"What became of King Richard?\" she asked presently." to "ready to go to dinner with us.\""
Also leave out the illustration caption at line 3585 ([Illustration: "A CLEVER SHEEP DOG." (SEE PRECEDING PAGE.)])
why_good: A quiet, reflective scene: a student at a well recites Richard II's two-buckets image to a small girl, the buckets change places as he talks, and she half-understands the metaphor of the deposed king as the bucket 'full of tears'. The reader has to connect the literal buckets, the quoted figure of speech and the child's feelings, and to notice the narrator's foreshadowing ('If he had not come up just then, there would have been no story to tell'). The tone is gentle, with an undercurrent of melancholy.
suitability: Read the whole story (lines 3566-3700): Daisy then leans too far, falls into the well holding the rope, and is hauled up when her Newfoundland jumps onto the other bucket; everyone is fine, and the dog is honored. No graphic content. Cut 2 removes the line that the king may have been 'put to death'. FLAG: the excerpt quotes six lines of Shakespeare (Richard II), so a famous text sits inside an obscure passage. Drop this candidate if that counts against it.
fame: Charlotte M. Vaile was a minor juvenile writer; this is a numbered filler in a St. Nicholas dog-story series, never reprinted as far as I know.

title: The Child Singer
author: Laura Fitch
first_words: In a narrow dirty street in the most miserable part of the great city of
last_words: A strange excitement bore her up, and she felt no fatigue.
why_good: Pathos in place of comedy: a London street child with an untaught gift for song sings through the night to pay for her aunt's burial. A careful reader must catch the narrator's judgments and ironies: 'loved as only a child or a woman can love one from whom she receives no sign of affection', 'Miserable as such a life was, it might have been worse', and the rough neighbors who are 'not hard-hearted' but have money only from what they 'earned or stole'. Also the contrast between the slum and 'the London which the world knows'. Somber and tender, the opposite of the P1 tone.
suitability: Read the whole story (lines 1176-1252): a great musician takes her in and she becomes a famous singer. The aunt's death (run over by a carriage, 'brought home on a shutter') is one sentence, not graphic. No caricature. Weakness: the ending is conventional and the story leans sentimental, which is why it ranks last.
fame: Laura Fitch is an unknown Harper's Young People contributor; the piece is obscure.

title: Kensington Clover
author: Marcia D. Bradbury
first_words: Such a hubbub in the meadow! / Such a rustling in the grass!
last_words: Tossed their pretty heads and said they / Wouldn't worry any more.
why_good: The whole poem: meadow flowers gossip in indignation at being copied in fashionable embroidery ('worked in colored worsted', 'a head on canvas'), with a poppy's pun on crewel/cruel and a clover's vanity, until a humble yellow violet asks whether the copies have fragrance or can renew themselves. A careful reader must infer the situation (Kensington needlework) from the clues, follow several distinct voices and attitudes, catch the pun and the irony, and identify the violet's argument about real versus imitation. Light satire in a playful tone.
suitability: Whole poem read. Nothing unsuitable. 'an innocent' in stanza 2 is a flower name (bluets), which might need a gloss.
fame: Marcia D. Bradbury is an unknown magazine versifier; the poem is a Harper's Young People filler.

title: Dear Me!
author: Margaret Eytinge
first_words: A grasshopper lay in the garden one day, / Near a cabbage--I mean cabbage-rose--
last_words: As I think with good reason it might-- / Dear me! / With the very best reason it might.
why_good: A mock elegy with a twist: Mrs. Sparrow mourns a dead grasshopper and solemnly promises to 'bury' him, then swallows him, and the cabbage-rose laughs. The reader has to catch the double meaning of 'bury', the shift from mock-pathos to dark comedy, the speaker's sly asides ('I mean cabbage-rose'), and the coinages ('doornailedly dead', 'incurvated'), plus the refrain whose tone changes from stanza to stanza.
suitability: Whole poem read. A bird eating an already-dead insect is natural, not cruelty. Nothing unsuitable.
fame: Margaret Eytinge was a prolific but now forgotten children's versifier; this poem is not anthologized. Her other piece in these files ('I'm a Little Story', pg23926) is not used.

title: Daisy-Song
author: Grace Denio Litchfield
first_words: I am only a plain little daisy-flower, / Sprung up at hap-hazard 'neath sunshine and shower,
last_words: And I keep my dress clean, my gold heart in its place, / And who is so happy as I?
why_good: A dramatic monologue whose cheerfulness is tested: the daisy admits hot days, cold nights, greener meadows, a brook it cannot see and stars out of reach, then decides each time not to repine. The refrain's conjunction changes from stanza to stanza (Yet / And / For / But / And), which signals concession against affirmation. A careful reader must weigh whether the contentment is naive or chosen ('I just look up at Fate with my brave little face'), and read the figurative 'white dress' and 'gold heart'.
fame: Grace Denio Litchfield was a minor novelist and poet, little read today; the poem is a St. Nicholas filler.
